name: Nesselwängle
kurzbeschreibung: Peaceful village at the Hahnenkamm with a ski area and a stunning Alpensee.
text:
Overview

Nesselwängle is situated in the Außerfern region of the Reutte district at the eastern portal of the Tannheim Valley, directly on the eastern shore of scenic Lake Haldensee at an altitude of 1,136 meters. Home to roughly 470 residents, the municipality comprises the primary village of Nesselwängle alongside the lakeside hamlet of Haller and the settlement of Rauth. This charming Alpine retreat occupies a sunny valley floor framed by the sheer limestone peaks of the Tannheim Mountains, notably the red-tinged Rote Flüh (2,108 m), the Gimpel (2,173 m), and the Kellenspitze (2,238 m). Recognized as a historic mountaineering village and premier rock climbing center, Nesselwängle seamlessly blends high-alpine crag climbing with refreshing watersports on a crystalline lake and peaceful family recreation.

History

The earliest documented mention of Nesselwängle dates to 1434 as 'Nesselwänglin', describing a small meadow overgrown with nettles. To distinguish it from the Bavarian market town of Nesselwang, the settlement was historically known as Klein Nesselwang. Guarding the eastern ascent over the Gaicht Pass, Nesselwängle played a vital role along the historic salt road, through which precious Hall in Tirol rock salt was carried across the Tannheim Valley into the Allgäu. From the late 19th century onwards, Nesselwängle made mountaineering history as the birthplace of extreme rock climbing in the Northern Limestone Alps, spearheaded by the famous first ascent of the Gimpel West Ridge in 1896. The Baroque parish church of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary, rebuilt following a devastating village fire in 1882, features splendid late 19th-century ceiling frescoes created by church painter Johann Kärle.

Getting There

Reaching Nesselwängle is remarkably convenient from both Austria and Germany. Arriving from southern Germany, motorists can travel toll-free via the A7 motorway exiting near Füssen/Pfronten through the Engetal, or via Kempten, Sonthofen, and the twisting Oberjoch Pass along the B199 Tannheimer Straße. From western Austria, the approach follows the A12 Inntal Autobahn and B179 Fernpass road to Reutte, continuing past Weißenbach am Lech and climbing the scenic Gaicht Pass straight into Nesselwängle. Rail passengers connect via Reutte in Tirol or Sonthofen (Allgäu) stations. From these railway hubs, regular VVT regional bus route 120 stops directly at Lake Haldensee, the Krinnenalp lift station, and village center.

Tips

Nesselwängle is world-renowned among mountaineers for the vertical limestone bastions of the Rote Flüh and Gimpel, offering legendary multi-pitch routes and the exhilarating Friedberger via ferrata, with welcoming rest stops at the Gimpelhaus and Tannheimer Hütte. Water lovers head to pristine Lake Haldensee, boasting drinking-water purity, rowing boat rentals, a flat 4.5-kilometer panoramic shoreline trail, and the solar-heated 'Wasserwelt Haldensee' lido with a 50-meter water slide. The Krinnenalpbahn chairlift whisks hikers and winter sports fans up to the Krinnenalpe on the Tennenberg, launching point for the Three Lakes View trail. In winter, the area provides natural-snow ski pistes, a speedy toboggan run, and immediate access to the 140-kilometer cross-country ski network.
